title: Regression Testing & CI for Agents
summary: A prompt tweak or model upgrade can quietly break behavior that used to work. Regression testing runs your curated eval set against the agent on every change — in CI, on a pull request — and fails the build when quality drops below a threshold. You compare new scores to a baseline, decide pass/fail with tolerances, and tame flaky LLM outputs with retries, aggregation, and seeded/mocked runs so the signal isn't drowned in noise.
nestedConcepts: the eval set as a test suite

subtopics.title: Regression testing vs a one-off eval
subtopics.explanation: A one-off eval tells you how good the agent is today; a regression test tells you whether a specific change made it worse than before. You freeze a known-good baseline score and, on each new prompt or model, re-score the same fixed dataset and compare. This diff-against-baseline framing is what lets CI catch a silent quality drop the moment it is introduced.
subtopics.example:
# one-off: just report today's score
score = evaluate(agent, dataset)
print(f"accuracy = {score:.2%}")

# regression: compare against a frozen baseline
BASELINE = 0.91          # locked in from the last green build
score = evaluate(agent, dataset)
regressed = score < BASELINE - 0.02   # 2pt tolerance
print("REGRESSION" if regressed else "ok", f"{score:.2%}")

subtopics.title: Treat the eval set as a test suite
subtopics.explanation: Each labeled example becomes a test case, and each scorer (exact match, LLM judge, tool-trajectory check) becomes an assertion over that case. You run them the way you run unit tests — parametrized, isolated, and reported per-case — so a failure points at the exact input that broke. Modeling evals as tests is what lets you reuse pytest, its fixtures, and its CI integration instead of building a bespoke harness.

subtopics.title: Thresholds and baselines decide pass/fail
subtopics.explanation: You rarely demand a perfect score; you require staying at or above a baseline within a tolerance band, because LLM scores wobble slightly even when nothing regressed. The build fails only when the drop exceeds the tolerance, and the baseline is bumped forward deliberately when you ship a genuine improvement. Choosing the threshold is a product decision — too tight and every run flakes red, too loose and real regressions slip through.

subtopics.title: Flaky tests: retries, aggregation, seeding
subtopics.explanation: Even at temperature 0, judges and multi-step agents can give slightly different verdicts run to run, so a single sample makes a brittle test. You reduce variance by running each case a few times and aggregating (majority vote or mean), pinning temperature and any seed you can, and mocking the model where the logic — not the generation — is what you're testing. Managing flakiness is what separates a CI gate people trust from one they learn to ignore.

subtopics.title: Wire it into CI on every change
subtopics.explanation: The whole point is automation: a workflow triggers on pull requests and runs the eval suite, blocking merge if the gate fails and posting the score diff as a check. You cache the frozen dataset, budget the model calls, and often run a fast subset per commit plus the full set nightly. Putting the gate in CI is what makes regression testing continuous rather than something a human remembers to do before release.
subtopics.example:
# .github/workflows/agent-eval.yml (conceptual)
# on: pull_request
# jobs:
#   eval:
#     steps:
#       - run: pytest tests/agent_evals -q   # fast subset
#       - run: python -m evals.gate --baseline 0.91 --tol 0.02
# a failing gate marks the PR check red and blocks merge
print("CI runs the eval suite and fails the build on regression")

foundations.overview: Agents are unusually easy to break silently: a reworded system prompt, a new tool description, or a provider model upgrade can shift behavior that had been working, and nothing throws an error — the quality just quietly drops. Regression testing closes that gap by treating your curated eval set as a test suite that runs automatically on every prompt or model change, typically in CI on each pull request. You lock a known-good baseline score, re-run the fixed dataset against the changed agent, and compare: if the score falls below the baseline by more than a chosen tolerance, the build fails and the change is blocked. Because LLM outputs are noisy even at temperature 0, a naive single-sample test flakes constantly, so you damp variance with repeated runs and aggregation, pin temperature and seeds, and mock the model wherever you're testing your own logic rather than the generation. Modeling all of this on top of pytest lets you reuse fixtures, parametrization, and existing CI plumbing instead of inventing a harness. The result is a gate that turns invisible quality regressions into loud, blocking test failures at exactly the moment they're introduced.
foundations.formalDefinition: Agent regression testing is the automated re-evaluation of an agent against a fixed, labeled dataset on every code, prompt, or model change, comparing the resulting aggregate score to a frozen baseline within a tolerance and failing the build (a CI gate) when the score regresses beyond that tolerance; flakiness is controlled via repeated sampling and aggregation, seed/temperature pinning, and model mocking.
foundations.whyItMatters: Prompt and model changes are the most common and least visible causes of agent quality loss, and they ship constantly. A CI regression gate is the only scalable way to catch a drop before users do, turning a class of silent, hard-to-attribute failures into deterministic, blocking, git-bisectable events.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of it exactly like unit tests for a codebase, but the 'function under test' is a probabilistic agent. Each labeled example is a test case, each scorer is an assertion, the baseline is the golden expected value, the tolerance is a fuzzy-equality epsilon that accounts for LLM noise, and CI is the gate that won't let a red suite merge.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Teams gate prompt-template PRs on an eval suite, run the full set nightly and a fast subset per commit, block model-version bumps until the suite stays green, and post score diffs as PR checks so reviewers see the quality impact of a change before approving it.
foundations.performanceImpact: Every eval case is one or more model calls, so a large suite is slow and costly to run on each commit; teams mitigate with a tiered strategy (small fast subset per PR, full suite nightly), caching of immutable datasets and prompt prefixes, and parallel execution, trading some coverage-per-commit for acceptable CI latency and cost.
commonUseCases: Gating prompt/template changes on a pull request
Blocking a provider model upgrade until scores hold
Nightly full-suite runs with per-commit fast subsets
Posting score diffs vs baseline as a PR status check

commonMisconceptions.myth: A regression test should require a perfect (100%) score.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Scores wobble run to run, so you gate on staying within a tolerance of a baseline, not on perfection. Demanding perfection makes the suite flake red constantly and teaches people to ignore it.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Temperature 0 makes agent tests deterministic, so one run is enough.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Temperature 0 reduces but does not eliminate variance — judges, tool timing, and provider nondeterminism still shift results. You still aggregate multiple runs to get a stable signal.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Regression testing means running the whole eval set on every commit.
commonMisconceptions.reality: That's usually too slow and expensive. Teams run a fast representative subset per commit and the full suite nightly or pre-release, balancing coverage against CI cost and latency.

interactiveExamples.title: A baseline gate that fails the build on a regression
interactiveExamples.explanation: Score the agent on a fixed dataset, then compare the aggregate to a frozen baseline within a tolerance. The gate raises (nonzero exit) only when the drop exceeds tolerance — exactly how a CI step blocks a merge.

code.caption: The first change dips slightly but stays inside the 2-point tolerance and passes; the second drops far below baseline and the gate raises, which in CI turns the PR check red.

interactiveExamples.title: Damping flaky judges with repeated sampling
interactiveExamples.explanation: A single judged run is noisy, so majority-voting or averaging several samples yields a stable score. Here a jittery judge that sometimes misfires is aggregated across runs so one bad sample doesn't fail the gate.

code.code:
import random
from statistics import mean

random.seed(0)   # make the demo reproducible

def flaky_judge():
    # a truly-correct case the judge scores 1.0 ~80% of the time,
    # occasionally misfiring to 0.0 (LLM-judge noise)
    return 1.0 if random.random() < 0.8 else 0.0

def stable_score(run_once, n=5):
    return mean(run_once() for _ in range(n))

single = flaky_judge()                 # could be a fluke 0.0
aggregated = stable_score(flaky_judge, n=5)

print("single sample:", single)
print("aggregated (n=5):", round(aggregated, 2))
print("gate on aggregate >= 0.7:", aggregated >= 0.7)
code.caption: The single sample can flip to 0.0 by chance; averaging five runs recovers the true ~0.8 signal so the gate is stable rather than flaky.
code.expectedOutput:
single sample: 1.0
aggregated (n=5): 0.8
gate on aggregate >= 0.7: True

codeLab.title: Build a regression gate with tolerance and aggregation
codeLab.instructions: Implement run_regression(cases, agent, baseline, tol=0.02, samples=3) that, for each case in cases, runs agent(case['input']) `samples` times, scores each run with score_fn(output, case['gold']) returning 1.0 for a correct tool choice else 0.0, averages the per-case samples, then averages across cases into a suite score. It must return a dict {'score': float, 'passed': bool} where passed is True iff score >= baseline - tol. Do NOT raise inside the function — the caller (CI) decides what to do with 'passed'. Complete the function so the harness passes.

solution.code:
from statistics import mean

def score_fn(output, gold):
    # 1.0 if the agent chose the expected tool, else 0.0
    return 1.0 if output == gold else 0.0

def run_regression(cases, agent, baseline, tol=0.02, samples=3):
    per_case = []
    for case in cases:
        # sample multiple runs to damp per-run LLM noise
        runs = [score_fn(agent(case["input"]), case["gold"])
                for _ in range(samples)]
        per_case.append(mean(runs))
    # suite score = mean of per-case averages
    score = mean(per_case)
    passed = score >= baseline - tol   # tolerance band, not perfection
    return {"score": score, "passed": passed}

codeLab.testHarness:
# a deterministic fake agent that always picks the right tool
def good_agent(inp):
    return {"refund order A-1": "issue_refund",
            "where is order A-2": "track_order"}[inp]

cases = [
    {"input": "refund order A-1", "gold": "issue_refund"},
    {"input": "where is order A-2", "gold": "track_order"},
]

res = run_regression(cases, good_agent, baseline=0.91)
assert res["score"] == 1.0 and res["passed"] is True

# a regressed agent that always picks the wrong tool
def bad_agent(inp):
    return "wrong_tool"

res2 = run_regression(cases, bad_agent, baseline=0.91)
assert res2["score"] == 0.0 and res2["passed"] is False
print("all tests passed")
hints: Build the per-case average first with statistics.mean over `samples` calls, then take the mean of those averages for the suite score.
The pass check is a single comparison: score >= baseline - tol; return it as the 'passed' boolean rather than raising.
Keep the function side-effect free so CI can log the score and decide whether to fail the build itself.

checkpoints.prompt: Why does a regression gate compare to a baseline within a tolerance rather than requiring a perfect score?
options: Perfect scores are impossible for any model
LLM scores wobble run to run, so a tolerance avoids flaking red on noise while still catching real drops
Tolerances make the tests run faster
The OpenAI API requires a tolerance parameter
checkpoints.explanation: Even at temperature 0, judges and multi-step agents vary slightly. A baseline-minus-tolerance gate passes on harmless noise and fails only on a genuine regression, which keeps the signal trustworthy.

checkpoints.prompt: This CI eval test is flaky and fails randomly. What's the root cause?
options: It scores a single case with a single sample and asserts exact equality, so any LLM-judge noise fails the build
checkpoints.explanation: One case, one sample, and an exact-equality assertion give the test no tolerance for normal LLM variance. Aggregate multiple samples across many cases and gate on a threshold, not exact equality.
baseline - tol = 0.91 - 0.02 = 0.89, and 0.895 >= 0.89, so the gate returns PASS — the small dip is within the tolerance band.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the aggregation so one flaky sample doesn't decide the case's score.
checkpoints.explanation: Averaging (mean) several samples damps single-run noise so the per-case score reflects the agent's typical behavior rather than one lucky or unlucky generation.

theory.question: What is agent regression testing, and how does it differ from a one-off evaluation?
theory.directAnswer: A one-off eval measures how good the agent is right now; regression testing automatically re-scores a fixed labeled dataset on every prompt or model change and compares the result to a frozen baseline, failing the build when the score drops beyond a tolerance. It answers 'did this change make things worse?' rather than 'how good is it?', and it runs continuously in CI rather than once.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Automated re-evaluation of an agent against a fixed eval set on each change, with a baseline-versus-tolerance gate that blocks regressions.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Prompt edits and model upgrades silently shift agent behavior without throwing errors, so quality can degrade unnoticed between releases.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: You freeze a known-good baseline score, re-run the same dataset against the changed agent (aggregating multiple samples to damp noise), compare the suite score to baseline minus tolerance, and fail CI if it regresses.

theory.whyImportant: It converts the most common cause of agent quality loss — invisible prompt/model drift — into a loud, blocking, bisectable CI failure at the moment it's introduced.
theory.realWorldExample: A team bumps their provider to a new model version; the regression suite drops from 0.91 to 0.78 on the tool-selection dataset, the PR check goes red, and they hold the upgrade until they re-tune the prompt.

followUps.question: How do you set the tolerance?
followUps.answer: Empirically: measure the run-to-run variance of your suite on an unchanged agent, then set tolerance a bit above that noise band so normal wobble passes but real drops fail.

followUps.question: When do you move the baseline?
followUps.answer: Only on a deliberate, verified improvement — you bump the baseline forward in the same PR so future runs are gated against the new, higher bar.

theory.question: How do you keep agent regression tests from being flaky in CI?
theory.directAnswer: Reduce variance at the source and aggregate what remains: pin temperature to 0 and any available seed, mock the model where you're testing your own logic rather than generation, run each case multiple times and aggregate (mean or majority vote), and gate on a tolerance band instead of exact equality so normal LLM noise doesn't flip the build red.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A set of techniques to make probabilistic agent tests produce a stable, trustworthy pass/fail signal in CI.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: LLM outputs and judges vary run to run even at temperature 0, so single-sample, exact-match tests fail randomly and erode trust in the suite.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Pin temperature/seed and mock the model for logic tests; for behavior tests, sample each case n times and aggregate; compare the aggregate to baseline within a tolerance; optionally quarantine or retry a small set of known-jittery cases.

theory.whyImportant: A flaky suite gets ignored or bypassed, defeating the purpose; a stable one is trusted enough to actually block merges, which is the whole point of a gate.
theory.realWorldExample: A judge misfired to 0.0 on ~20% of runs, so a single-sample test flaked; averaging five samples per case recovered the true ~0.8 signal and the gate stopped failing at random.

followUps.question: Why not just raise the retry count until it's green?
followUps.answer: Blind retries multiply cost and latency and can mask a real regression; you want to fix variance at the source and aggregate deliberately, not paper over it.

followUps.question: When should you mock the model entirely?
followUps.answer: When the test targets your orchestration/parsing/routing logic rather than generation quality — mocking makes those tests deterministic and fast.

scenario.question: Your team ships prompt changes several times a day and keeps discovering quality regressions only after users complain. Design a CI setup that catches them earlier without making the pipeline unbearably slow or expensive.
scenario.directAnswer: Turn the eval set into a pytest suite with a baseline gate, and run a fast representative subset on every PR plus the full suite nightly and pre-release. Aggregate a few samples per case to control flakiness, gate on baseline-minus-tolerance, cache the immutable dataset and prompt prefixes, run cases in parallel, and post the score diff as a PR check that blocks merge on a real regression.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A tiered CI regression strategy balancing coverage-per-commit against latency and model-call cost.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Running the whole eval set on every commit is too slow and costly, but running nothing lets regressions reach users, so you split coverage across triggers.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Pick a small stratified subset covering the main behaviors for per-PR runs, keep the full labeled set for nightly/pre-release, share a baseline and tolerance, aggregate samples, cache datasets and prefixes, parallelize, and surface the score delta on the PR.

scenario.whyImportant: It moves regression detection from 'after users complain' to 'before merge' while keeping CI cost and time acceptable, which is what makes the gate sustainable day to day.
scenario.realWorldExample: A team added a 40-case per-PR subset (aggregated over 3 samples) plus a 600-case nightly run; a prompt refactor that would have degraded refunds tripped the PR check within minutes and never reached production.

followUps.question: How do you choose the per-PR subset?
followUps.answer: Stratify by behavior/intent so each major capability is represented, and include known past-regression cases as canaries; keep it small enough to run in a couple of minutes.

followUps.question: How do you keep the full suite affordable nightly?
followUps.answer: Cache the dataset and fixed prompt prefixes, parallelize case execution, and use a cheaper judge model where the task allows, reserving the strong judge for borderline cases.

coding.question: Write a function that runs a labeled eval set against an agent, aggregates multiple samples per case to reduce noise, and returns whether the suite passed a baseline gate within a tolerance.
coding.thoughtProcess: I need per-case stability, so I sample each case n times and average. The suite score is the mean of per-case averages. The pass decision is a single comparison against baseline minus tolerance. I return the score and a boolean rather than raising, so the CI caller decides how to fail the build; this keeps the function pure and testable.
lineByLine: For each case we call the agent `samples` times and score each run with the caller-supplied score_fn.
statistics.mean collapses the per-case samples into one number that reflects typical behavior rather than a single run.
The suite score is the mean of the per-case averages, giving every case equal weight.
The pass decision is score >= baseline - tol, returned as a boolean so the function stays pure.
Returning a dict (score + passed) lets CI log the number and decide whether to exit nonzero, keeping side effects out of the scorer.
The __main__ block wires a deterministic fake agent and scorer so the example runs standalone.
coding.timeComplexity: O(cases * samples) agent calls, each dominated by one model round-trip.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(cases) for the per-case averages held during the run.

followUps.question: How would you turn this into a failing CI step?
followUps.answer: Call run_suite, log the score, and `sys.exit(0 if result['passed'] else 1)` so a False raises a nonzero exit that fails the job and blocks merge.

followUps.question: How would you report per-case regressions, not just the suite score?
followUps.answer: Return the per_case list keyed by case id and diff each against a stored per-case baseline so the report pinpoints which inputs regressed.

keyTakeaways: Regression testing re-scores a fixed eval set on every prompt/model change and asks 'did this make it worse?' — not just 'how good is it?'
Model evals as a test suite: each labeled case is a test, each scorer an assertion, so you reuse pytest, fixtures, and CI plumbing.
Gate on a frozen baseline within a tolerance, never on a perfect score, so normal LLM noise passes but real drops fail the build.
Tame flakiness by pinning temperature/seed, mocking the model for logic tests, and aggregating multiple samples per case.
Wire it into CI with a fast per-PR subset plus a nightly full run, caching and parallelizing to keep cost and latency sustainable.
